Lessons.Title: Generalize Fraction Multiplication
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: move from a fully gridded fraction-area diagram to multiplying two fractions without requiring every unit cell to be drawn. The 2021 source makes the scaffolding optional by stages and asks children to decide when a sketch is useful, including unusually large denominators.

Warm-up: compare two diagrams for a 4/5-by-1/2 rectangular region, one with twenty equal cells and another labelled only with side lengths. Explain why 8/20, 4/10 and 2/5 describe the same area despite different partitions.

Activity 1 — three original products: 2/5×3/4=6/20=3/10, then 3/7×4/5=12/35, then 9/11×5/8=45/88. For the first, draw a five-column-by-four-row whole; for the second choose a sketch or counting; for the third use the numerator/denominator structure when physically drawing 88 parts is inefficient. Explain the benefit and limits of each choice.

Activity 2 — Multiply Fractions (source, not a free discussion-only critique): solve (3/8)×(2/5)=6/40, (3/4)×(9/5)=27/20 and (10/5)×(6/5)=60/25. Then determine the missing factor in (8/9)×?=56/36 (answer 7/4) and 5×?=15/8 (answer 3/8). Show why the inverse multiplication structure works. Source Activity 1 2/5×3/4, 3/7×4/5, 9/11×5/8 and Diego's diagram remain covered.

Source boundary: strategies for diagram choice, a correct visual partition, commutativity and explanation are teacher reviewed. Numeric product checks do not establish whether learners understand fraction-area structure; original teacher image cards are not copied.

Original 2021 warm-up two equivalent 4/5-by-1/2 figures display 8/20 and 4/10. Children may defend the equality from partitioning 2/4=1/2. Teacher reviews the source figures, requested diagrams, estimate of product magnitude and students' decisions to use a grid for 45/88, not merely the selected numeric choice.

KeyConcepts.Title: Product independent of diagram density
KeyConcepts.Definition: A fraction product can be found by counting selected cells over all cells or by equivalent exact multiplication.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For valid fractions a/b and c/d, the product ac/bd.

KeyConcepts.Title: Optional representation
KeyConcepts.Definition: A full grid is one tool, not an obligation when denominators make many cells.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Choose a diagram, decomposition or an abstract product if the reasoning is clear.
KeyConcepts.Example: Drawing 88 tiny cells may be less useful than naming 9×5 and 11×8.

KeyConcepts.Title: Equivalent area fractions
KeyConcepts.Definition: Repartitioning into a finer equal grid can preserve area.
KeyConcepts.Example: Both drawings with dimensions 4/5 and 1/2 give area 2/5.

WorkedExamples.Title: Compute with a grid
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 2/5×3/4.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party mathematical model with an explicit reasoning check.
Steps: Partition whole into five columns and four rows.
Shade two columns across three selected rows, giving six cells.
Compare with 20 total cells and simplify.

WorkedExamples.Title: Choose an efficient method
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 3/7×4/5.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party mathematical model with an explicit reasoning check.
Steps: Identify three selected rows out of seven and four columns out of five.
Write the exact product without needing every cell drawn.
WorkedExamples.Check: Both factors are below one, and 12/35 is also below one.

WorkedExamples.Title: Large denominator product
WorkedExamples.Question: Find 9/11×5/8.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party mathematical model with an explicit reasoning check.
Steps: Explain that a detailed 88-cell sketch is optional.
WorkedExamples.Check: Multiplying across gives 45/88 and the result is below both factors.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source Activity 2: product of two fractions
WorkedExamples.Question: Calculate (3/8)×(2/5), (3/4)×(9/5) and (10/5)×(6/5).
WorkedExamples.Method: Exact numerator and denominator multiplication with unit-square interpretation.
WorkedExamples.Check: Values can be reduced to 3/20, 27/20, 12/5 without changing the source products.

WorkedExamples.Title: Source Activity 2: missing fraction factor
WorkedExamples.Question: Solve (8/9)×?=56/36 and 5×?=15/8.
WorkedExamples.Method: Use inverse multiplication or exact factor ratios; explain why the same whole is preserved.
Steps: Use 5×3/8=15/8 to find the second factor.
Substitute the missing fractions back and verify both equations.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Add rather than multiply the numerator/denominator counts
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A grid has rows times columns; adding their counts cannot describe a rectangular array.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count the product of row and column selections.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume a product is untrustworthy unless a full drawing is made
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Understanding the grid structure can justify exact fraction multiplication symbolically.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use an optional sketch or cell-count argument and check size against benchmarks.

SummaryPoints: Original warm-up equivalent 8/20=4/10=2/5 diagrams require visual justification.
Original Activity 2 three products 6/40, 27/20 and 60/25, followed by missing factors 7/4 and 3/8.
Numeric source choices support but do not replace teacher review of Diego's diagram and explanations.
Restricted publisher Cool-down is replaced by an independent Edulytiks teacher-scored fraction-equation explanation.

Lessons.Title: Apply Fraction Multiplication
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: apply exact fraction multiplication to the ACTUAL IM 2021 U03:L08 source flags. Measurements in inches are side lengths; results in square inches describe area. Teacher checks how each source flag image is interpreted. Foreign flag photos and logos are not copied because their third-party rights differ.

Warm-up — Number Talk Fraction Multiplication: the four exact source expressions are (1/3)×(3/5)=1/5, (2/3)×(3/5)=2/5, (5/3)×(3/5)=1 and (2/3)×(13/5)=26/15. Compare strategies with and without a visual area model.

Activity 1 — Flags: original Thailand flag replica measures 5 inches wide and 7 1/2 inches long. Total area = 5×7 1/2=37 1/2 square inches. Each red stripe is 5/6 inch wide, so its area is (5/6)×(7 1/2)=25/4 square inches; blue stripe width 10/6 inch yields 25/2 square inches. Explain how the striped source geometry relates to measured widths and areas (not an invented 8×6 1/2 banner).

Activity 2 — More Flags: in the source Colombia replica the flag is 3 1/2 inches wide and 5 1/4 inches long. Yellow occupies half the width, so its stripe width is 7/4 inches and its area is (7/4)×(21/4)=147/16 square inches. Blue and red each occupy one quarter of flag width, hence (1/4)×(3 1/2)=7/8 INCH (length, not area). The student must invent the appropriate QUESTION for the 7/8-inch and 147/16-square-inch calculations and justify why dimensions/units determine the question.

Synthesis and assessment: source flag graphics and red/blue/yellow region proportions remain teacher-reviewed, as do student-written questions and modeling. Exact numeric products support but cannot replace visual source interpretation. An independent Edulytiks flag-striped teacher Cool-down checks the same distinction; original publisher Cool-down and independent Student Task PDF were not separately inspected.
Existing 8-by-6 1/2 first-party banner examples are mathematically sound OPTIONAL EXTENSIONS, not IM 2021 source Activity 1 or 2.

KeyConcepts.Title: Area in a realistic context
KeyConcepts.Definition: Multiply the two perpendicular measured dimensions of a rectangular flag or stripe.
KeyConcepts.Example: One subregion of height 3/4 inch and width 8 inches is 6 square inches.

KeyConcepts.Title: Proportional stripes with fixed width
KeyConcepts.Definition: For stripes of the same length, doubling stripe height doubles area.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Area A=width×height; if height doubles and width stays fixed, area doubles.

KeyConcepts.Title: Mixed-number equivalence
KeyConcepts.Definition: A mixed-length area can be computed by decomposition or improper fraction.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original Thailand full flag
WorkedExamples.Question: Thailand replica is 5 inches by 7 1/2 inches. Find area.
WorkedExamples.Method: Mathematical product based on verified text of original flag activity; teacher reviews national flag figures and units.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original Thailand red and blue stripes
WorkedExamples.Question: Compute red stripe (5/6)×(15/2) and blue stripe (10/6)×(15/2).
WorkedExamples.Method: Mathematical product based on verified text of original flag activity; teacher reviews national flag figures and units.
WorkedExamples.Check: Double stripe width gives double stripe area.

WorkedExamples.Title: Original Colombia length versus area
WorkedExamples.Question: What questions are answered by (1/4)×3 1/2=7/8 and by (1/2×3 1/2)×(5 1/4)=147/16?
WorkedExamples.Method: Mathematical product based on verified text of original flag activity; teacher reviews national flag figures and units.
Steps: First expression is a blue/red stripe width (inches).
Second multiplies yellow stripe width 7/4 by flag length 21/4.
Second result is yellow stripe area (square inches).
WorkedExamples.Answer: 7/8 inch width; 147/16 square inches yellow area.
WorkedExamples.Check: Do not confuse length units with area units.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional extension — Whole banner
WorkedExamples.Question: A banner measures 8 inches by 6 1/2 inches. What is its area?
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party mathematical model with an explicit reasoning check.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional extension — Red stripe
WorkedExamples.Question: A stripe is 8 inches across and 3/4 inch high. What is its area?
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party mathematical model with an explicit reasoning check.
Steps: Identify the same 8-inch width as the banner.
Write square inches, not linear inches.

WorkedExamples.Title: Optional extension — Blue stripe
WorkedExamples.Question: A second stripe has the same width but height 1 1/2 inches. How does its area compare?
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party mathematical model with an explicit reasoning check.
Steps: Use double the red stripe area, 2×6.
WorkedExamples.Answer: 12 square inches, twice the red stripe's area.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Treat a stripe's height as its area
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Area measures the product of width and height.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use square units and the correct shared width.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Reuse protected publisher flag artwork without asset review
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: A public textbook page and its separate images can have different licenses and attribution requirements.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Use independently authored color-stripe models and verify each external asset separately.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Use an invented banner rather than original Thailand/Colombia tasks
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Original 2021 measurement numbers, flags and units determine different answers.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Keep first-party banners as optional extension after authentic source arithmetic and image interpretation.

SummaryPoints: Thailand replica 5×7 1/2 has area 37 1/2 square inches; red 25/4 and blue 25/2 square inches.
Colombia replica 3 1/2 by 5 1/4; blue/red width 7/8 inch, yellow area 147/16 square inches.
Original flags and student question interpretation require teacher review; never infer area from a stripe width alone.
Third-party flag image rights, original Student PDF and publisher-gated Cool-down remain unverified.

Lessons.Title: My Own Flag (optional)
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: independently DESIGN a symbolic banner and compute or estimate areas of its colored geometric components. The source's optional activity emphasizes creativity, constraints, measurement and open mathematical modeling, rather than one numeric product as the only answer.

Original source warm-up Notice and Wonder: discuss the FLAGS OF BOTSWANA AND TAIWAN shown in teacher-provided material, including color, shape and symbolism. The source public HTML attributes its original images to separate public-domain/CC0 providers; do not duplicate those images or claim pixel equivalence. Teacher reviews respectful questions and observations.

Original Activity 1 — Principles of Flag Design (MLR2 Collect and Display): Keep It Simple; Use Meaningful Symbolism; Use 2 to 3 Basic Colors; No Lettering or Seals; Be Distinctive or Be Related. The teacher assigns a principle to each partner group; learners discuss its meaning, compare source Botswana/Taiwan flags, create a shared language display, and justify multiple source-image design choices. First-party abstract designs are optional comparisons, not source substitutes.

Original Activity 2 — My Flag: learners use real paper, rulers and colored pencils/crayons to DESIGN THEIR OWN flag, explain symbols and colors, estimate or calculate how much fabric of EACH color they require in SQUARE INCHES, and exchange designs with a partner who critiques the five principles. The student chooses the measurements and geometric shapes; there is NO universal canonical area answer. A first-party 8 by 5 1/2 three-band banner with 10, 16 and 18 sq in bands is retained as a scaffold only, not original source requirements.

Activity 2 — critique alternative layouts: if a learner adds an overlapping emblem, the union of colored regions may not be the plain sum of each separate painted piece. Ask the designer to explain whether it is a new layer of color versus a separate piece of fabric. Compare another legitimate design with equal total area but a different shape arrangement.

Teacher assessment: creativity, symbolism, physical design, estimation for unusual shapes, checking overlaps and the explanatory reflection are inherently teacher-reviewed. Numeric checks validate a proposed design's measurements only, and MUST NOT mark the original optional flag project automatically complete. No national-flag artwork or protected source images were reused.

KeyConcepts.Title: Original flag design and area
KeyConcepts.Definition: A design has chosen dimensions and may contain colored partitions whose areas are calculated separately.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For nonoverlapping rectangles, total area is the sum of the component areas.
KeyConcepts.Example: Three bands of areas 10,16,18 cover 44 square inches.

KeyConcepts.Title: Component widths and heights
KeyConcepts.Definition: Each component must use side lengths that correspond to its actual extent.
KeyConcepts.Rule: A band 8 inches wide and 1 1/4 inches tall has area 10 square inches.

KeyConcepts.Title: Overlapping decoration
KeyConcepts.Definition: Colored layers or emblems do not necessarily increase the unique cloth area.
KeyConcepts.Rule: If pieces overlap, the union area needs a non-overlapping accounting.
KeyConcepts.Example: A badge painted on top of a banner does not add fabric area.

KeyConcepts.Title: Criteria and open-design critique
KeyConcepts.Definition: A design can be assessed for meaningful communication, distinctive structure and visual simplicity in addition to quantitative area.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Evaluate the actual learner design with a teacher rubric; a numeric calculation cannot score its meaning or aesthetic choices.
KeyConcepts.Example: A clear three-band pattern can satisfy a simplicity goal, but students still need to explain what the colors represent.

WorkedExamples.Title: Design a three-band banner
WorkedExamples.Question: Find area of an 8-by-5 1/2-inch banner with bands 1 1/4,2,2 1/4 inches tall.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party mathematical model with an explicit reasoning check.
Steps: Multiply the three band heights by the 8-inch width.

WorkedExamples.Title: Find a band area
WorkedExamples.Question: A band is 8 inches wide and 2 1/4 inches high. What area does it cover?
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party mathematical model with an explicit reasoning check.

WorkedExamples.Title: Check a mixed nonrectangular design
WorkedExamples.Question: A learner paints a small star over a colored banner stripe. Is the banner fabric larger just because the star is painted?
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party mathematical model with an explicit reasoning check.
Steps: Distinguish a separate fabric piece from pigment covering existing fabric.
Identify the actual physical boundary of the banner.
Recalculate fabric area using the banner's outer dimensions.
WorkedExamples.Answer: No. With a painted star the fabric area remains 44 square inches.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher checks the actual design; creative choices cannot be graded from one numeric answer.

WorkedExamples.Title: Critique a first-party design
WorkedExamples.Question: A student makes a three-band banner with simple colors and writes its name across the middle. Which design criterion might be reconsidered?
WorkedExamples.Method: Evaluate an independently described banner against simplicity and communicative criteria, without claiming one unique artistic answer.
Steps: Describe the layout and what the bands represent.
Explain why additional lettering may reduce clarity at a distance.
Offer a graphical alternative and justify whether it preserves the student's intended meaning.
WorkedExamples.Answer: A learner might replace lettering with a simple shape, while maintaining a meaningful design; other reasoned revisions are possible.
WorkedExamples.Check: Teacher reviews the actual drawing and explanation; no numeric auto-grader may mark this task as complete.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Add painted decoration as extra physical fabric area
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: Overlaying a color changes visual appearance, not the total underlying fabric.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Count only actual occupied nonoverlapping fabric regions for a total area.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Choose bands whose heights exceed the banner
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The component shapes must fit the outer dimensions and not double-count regions.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Sum heights and check they exactly match the planned banner height.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Automatically complete an original learner-designed flag using the numeric 44-square-inch sample
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The optional source permits arbitrary flag dimensions and non-rectangular geometry; the sample is only a scaffold.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Require teacher review of the learner's drawn original, measured colored regions and design-principle reflections.

SummaryPoints: The original optional U03:L09 is a student-directed flag DESIGN project, not a fixed-product exercise.
Original five principles: Keep It Simple, Use Meaningful Symbolism, Use 2 to 3 Basic Colors, No Lettering or Seals, Be Distinctive or Be Related.
Learners estimate actual needed colored fabric in square inches, then discuss a partner's symbols, meanings and design criteria.
Teacher reviews each unique flag drawing, geometric partition, overlapping colors and open explanation.
Supplemental 8×5 1/2 sample yields 44 square inches, not a teacher-approved score of the original project.

Lessons.Title: Concepts of Division (optional)
ExplanationParagraphs: Goal: compare equal-sharing quotients conceptually before formal work on division of a unit fraction by a whole number and a whole number by a unit fraction. The public 2021 source asks students to order multiple sharing situations and reason about how changes in the number of sharers or items affect a person's share.

Warm-up: compare 120 divided by 12,6,3 and 2. With the same dividend, a smaller positive divisor produces a greater quotient, and the reasoning should be stated in terms of group size or number of shares.

Activity 1 — original snack-sharing table: compare five situations with whole items: (A) four people share forty, (B) five people share forty-five, (C) five people share forty, (D) ten people share forty, (E) five people share fifteen. Order each person's shares: A=10, B=9, C=8, D=4, E=3, so A>B>C>D>E. Students may first reason comparatively without full calculation, and then check by exact quotients.

Activity 2: hold total fixed at 40 pieces and compare groups of 4,5,10; then hold people fixed at 5 and vary totals 15,40,45. Explain why quotient changes differently in each family and state the valid positivity assumptions. Use diagrams or verbal grouping when mathematical representations differ.

Assessment: the source's optional lesson uses open order/why explanations and develops future fraction-division concepts. Computing one numerical quotient is insufficient evidence of the original comparison/ordering task. Teacher reviews comparative explanations and group models; original pretzel photograph and gated Cool-down not copied.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fixed dividend, changing divisor
KeyConcepts.Definition: Sharing the same positive total among more people gives a smaller equal share.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For fixed a>0 and positive b<c, a/b>a/c.

KeyConcepts.Title: Fixed divisor, changing dividend
KeyConcepts.Definition: More objects shared by the same positive number of people give each person more.
KeyConcepts.Rule: For fixed b>0 and positive a<c, a/b<c/b.

KeyConcepts.Title: Ordering by share size
KeyConcepts.Definition: An equal-sharing situation can be compared by the quotient total divided by recipients.
KeyConcepts.Rule: Keep the contextual roles of dividend and divisor clear.
KeyConcepts.Example: 40 for 4 students ranks above 45 for 5 students.

WorkedExamples.Title: Order five sharing stories
WorkedExamples.Question: Sort 40÷4,45÷5,40÷5,40÷10,15÷5 from largest to smallest.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party mathematical model with an explicit reasoning check.
Steps: Find 15÷5=3 and order the distinct shares.

WorkedExamples.Title: Keep the total fixed
WorkedExamples.Question: Compare 40 items split among 4, 5 or 10 people.
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party mathematical model with an explicit reasoning check.
WorkedExamples.Answer: Four people receive the most; ten people the least.

WorkedExamples.Title: Keep the sharers fixed
WorkedExamples.Question: Five people share 15,40 or45 objects in three situations. Which gives the most?
WorkedExamples.Method: Original first-party mathematical model with an explicit reasoning check.
WorkedExamples.Answer: The 45-object situation gives 9 each, the greatest share.
WorkedExamples.Check: Every quotient uses the same five recipients.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Assume the greatest total always gives the largest share
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The number of recipients may also change, so the dividend alone cannot order all situations.
CommonMistakes.Correction: Compare both total quantity and recipient count, or compute quotients.

CommonMistakes.Mistake: Infer negative or zero divisor cases from positive sharing models
CommonMistakes.WhyWrong: The original fair-sharing context assumes a positive number of recipients.
CommonMistakes.Correction: State the positive-divisor requirement and preserve the context of equal real-world shares.

SummaryPoints: Increasing recipients for the same positive total decreases each share.
Increasing the total for the same positive number of people increases each share.
Comparing and defending the order of sharing situations is teacher-reviewed.
